source_text: Sed non tua opinio apud prudentes tantum valebit, ut, cum tu sis caput horum et causa malorum [n143] , de conflictu medio Apostoli te obiectione subducas et putes illum pro te esse feriendum, quo potissimum contra vos praeceptore armamur ac principe. Ut ergo, quid tibi dicendum sit, consequenter agnoscas; si mihi et tibi super hoc esset nulla dissensio, quod Apostolus naturali peccato Manichaeorum dogma firmaret, tunc tuum caput petenti illum constanter opponeres; nunc vero, cum inviolabilis apud me Magistri Gentium dignitas perseveret eiusque verba tua laedi expositione non patiar, quae secundum regulam prolatam rationis stulto, impuro et impio assero dogmati repugnare nihilque eum pro peccato naturali dixisse convinco, qua tu impudentia ingeris, ut vel pro te mihi ille respondeat, qui non interrogatur, quoniam nec de eius sapientia dubitatur, vel me vociferaris nolle audire ab Apostolo, quod in te ab Apostolo nobis tradita intellegentiae sanitate detestor?
pass_a_gloss: But your opinion will not avail so much among the prudent that, when you are the head of these and the cause of evils, you withdraw yourself from the middle of the conflict by an objection of the Apostle and think that he is to be struck for you, with which teacher and prince we are especially armed against you. That you may therefore recognize consequently what is to be said to you; if there were for me and you no disagreement over this, that the Apostle confirmed the Manichaeans' dogma by a natural sin, then you would constantly set him against one seeking your head; but now, when the dignity of the Teacher of the Gentiles remains inviolable with me and I do not suffer his words to be injured by your exposition, which according to the rule of reason brought forth I assert are repugnant to a foolish, impure, and impious dogma and I convict him to have said nothing for a natural sin, with what shamelessness do you thrust in that either he answer me for you, who is not questioned, since neither is it doubted about his wisdom, or you cry out that I am unwilling to hear from the Apostle what I detest in you by the soundness of understanding handed down to us by the Apostle?

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: But your opinion will not carry such weight among the wise that, although you are ‘the source and cause of these evils’ (Virgil, Aeneid 11.361), you can withdraw from the middle of the contest by putting the apostle in the way. You suppose that he should take the blows for you, although he is precisely the teacher and leader who arms us against you. To understand, then, what you can consistently say: if you and I agreed that the apostle confirmed the Manichaeans’ doctrine of natural sin, you could confidently place him in the path of someone aiming at your head. As it is, however, the Teacher of the Gentiles’ dignity remains inviolable for me. I will not permit your interpretation to injure his words, which, according to the rule of reason set out above, I maintain are opposed to a foolish, filthy, and impious doctrine. I prove that he said nothing in favor of natural sin. With what shamelessness, then, do you insist that he answer me in your place, when he is not being questioned because his wisdom is not doubted? Or how do you shout that I refuse to hear from the apostle what I detest in you precisely through the sound understanding the apostle has handed down to us?

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
